newsitem.title: USA: Simpson lawyers to stress evidence planting.
newsitem.headline: Simpson lawyers to stress evidence planting.

text.p: O.J. Simpson's lead attorney Wednesday told prospective jurors in the civil trial of his client that he intended to confront police officers on the witness stand to prove his theory that evidence was planted.

Robert Baker made it clear that, as in Simpson's criminal case, the thrust of the defence would be that one or more officers planted evidence to incriminate the former football star and that other evidence was tampered with or deliberately contaminated.

He said he would be asking officers and FBI experts tough and confrontational questions to prove his point, and asked the prospective panellists if they would be comfortable with that. Most said they would.

Simpson, who became a TV sports commentator and Hollywood actor after his football career, was found not guilty by a criminal court jury last year of the June 12, 1994, stabbing murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman.
He is now fighting a civil wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.
The prospective panel changed a number of times in the most active day of jury selection since the process started on Sept. 20.

Three jurors were excused during the morning -- a white woman who said her son's soccer team was coached by a friend of Simpson and another white woman who was a park ranger and would-be police officer who said she did not believe a police officer would plant or tamper with evidence.

A black woman postal worker was excused when she said she had an action pending against her white supervisor who she alleges assaulted her when the not guilty verdict in Simpson's criminal trial was announced last October.
During the afternoon, when lawyers were allowed peremptory challenges without having to say why they wanted a juror excused, four black women and one white women were let go.

Attorneys for the plaintiffs excused the four black women, prompting Baker to ask Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki for a closed door meeting, where he filed a motion claiming the plaintiffs were using their peremptory challenges purely on the basis of race. Fujisaki denied the motion.

Midway through the afternoon session, the make-up of the prospective panel was seven whites, three blacks and two Latinos. Race has proved to be an important issue in the civil trial, as it was in the criminal trial. Simpson is black, the two victims were white.
